extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, and math educators interested in proof exposition and style
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the stylistic choices in mathematical writing or proofs (e.g., geometric vs algebraic, constructive vs classical), their consistency, and their fit to audience, pedagogy, and the theorem's content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to a recognized stylistic tradition (Chevalley's eras)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a piece of mathematics adheres consistently to a recognizable tradition (e.g., the 19th-century 'ε-style' of Weierstrassian rigor with inequalities and careful quantifier order vs the 20th-century 'axiomatic style' that is definition-first and suppresses computational detail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate if the work is identifiable as belonging to a tradition or if it mixes traditions in a way that confuses readers. Anti-pattern: inconsistent switching between ε-style calculations and axiomatic, structure-first presentation without signaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of introduction (Granger)
rubrics_metrics.description: How concepts are introduced: via examples, axioms, motivating problems, or counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the chosen mode of introduction suits the material and target reader (e.g., novices may benefit from examples and motivating problems; specialists may prefer axioms). Note that different introductions preserve truth but change cognitive accessibility and pedagogical fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of connection (Granger)
rubrics_metrics.description: How one concept is linked to neighboring concepts — by definition, by theorem, by analogy, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check clarity and appropriateness of connective strategies. Effective connection can aid transfer and generalization; poor connections can leave concepts isolated or obscure the conceptual landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of unification (Granger)
rubrics_metrics.description: What organizing principle ties the concepts together (e.g., a structural framework, a common motivating problem, or an analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a clear unifying principle is presented and whether it helps the reader see the relations among results. Lack of unification may impede understanding and limit generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutive role of style (Hacking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness that a style of reasoning can introduce new objects of inquiry and that objects may not be independent of the style that brings them into view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging work, take into account the stylistic tradition that defines what the relevant objects and questions are. Avoid purely 'intrinsic' judgments that ignore how style shapes the problems considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric vs. algebraic axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether proofs/reasoning proceed via figures, spatial intuition, and geometric constructions versus symbol manipulation and algebraic computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider which mode better illuminates the theorem; geometric approaches may offer visualization and intuition, algebraic ones may offer generality and formal manipulability. Ensure consistency with intended claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual vs. computational axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the argument appeals to structural, conceptual insight or to explicit calculation and computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match style to the theorem's nature: structural claims often suit conceptual proofs; computational claims may legitimately use calculation. Avoid using heavy computation to prove something whose essence is conceptual unless it aids understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural vs. intuitive axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the presentation appeals primarily to axioms and formal structure or to mental images and intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how well the chosen balance supports reader comprehension. Intuitive accounts can be pedagogically powerful but should be backed by structural clarity when rigor is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs. methodological axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the style is tied to specific communities, national traditions, or particular practices (local) versus part of a universal method shared across contexts (methodological).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sensitive to audience: a locally-inflected style may be natural to a community but perplexing to outsiders. Where methodological universality matters, prefer styles that make methods explicit and transferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive vs. classical axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether existence is exhibited (constructive) or shown indirectly/non-constructively (classical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a constructive proof is required (pedagogy, computation, foundational stance) or whether classical reasoning suffices. Make explicit which commitment is being used, since this affects what counts as a satisfactory proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthetic vs. analytic axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the proof builds forward from premises (synthetic) or decomposes from the goal (analytic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider which approach clarifies the argument and whether the chosen direction aligns with readers' expectations. Mixing approaches is permissible if clearly justified and not misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization (Tappenden)
rubrics_metrics.description: What a proof allows the reader to see — the mental or diagrammatic images that the argument supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the proof affords useful visualizations that aid understanding and whether those visualizations are made explicit. Anti-pattern: relying on implicit visual intuition without explanation, which can mislead or exclude some readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification (Tappenden)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which other results the proof groups with — the extent to which the style reveals connections across theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the chosen presentation facilitates recognizing families of results and transferring techniques. A style that isolates a theorem without showing relations may reduce its explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom choice (Tappenden)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which background commitments or axioms the proof activates and depends upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the dependence on particular axioms is made explicit and that the style aligns with or justifies those commitments; different axiom choices can change what is acceptable or illuminating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifiability of stylistic tradition (implied rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the piece's stylistic tradition identifiable (geometric, axiomatic, constructive, etc.) or does it shift confusingly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clarity about the guiding tradition. If mixing traditions, signal and justify transitions; unexplained shifts are an anti-pattern that can impede reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitness of modes (implied rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether modes of introduction, connection, and unification are made explicit in the exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly stating how concepts are introduced and connected helps readers navigate the material. Good practice: state your organizing principles and the intended conceptual path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit to intended reader (implied rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the chosen style maximizes understanding for the intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audience needs (students, specialists, interdisciplinary readers) and choose modes and levels of detail accordingly. Pedagogical clarity may trump methodological purity depending on goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with theorem's content (implied rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the style chosen is appropriate to the nature of the theorem (e.g., not using a primarily computational style to make a structural point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mismatch between method and goal. If an unconventional style is used, provide rationale and discuss advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of alternative styles (implied rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the exposition acknowledges that other proofs/styles exist (e.g., 'there is also a geometric proof').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noting alternatives situates the work and helps readers see trade-offs. Failure to acknowledge common alternatives can obscure the scope and novelty of the presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability conditions for style critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations in which style critique is most relevant: when the same theorem admits multiple styles, when pedagogical clarity is a goal, or when methodological purity is at stake (e.g., using complex analysis to prove number-theoretic results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before judging style, check whether style is an adjustable variable in the context. If style is the only difference between proofs, stylistic criteria are especially salient; otherwise stylistic critique may be less relevant.
